enonce_intro_markdown:
Two particles $P$ and $Q$, of masses $6\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $4\ \mathrm{kg}$ respectively, are connected by a light inextensible string of length $2\ \mathrm{m}$. The string passes over a light smooth pulley fixed at the top of a smooth plane which is inclined at an angle $\alpha$ to the horizontal, where $\sin\alpha = \tfrac35$. Initially, the particles are held at rest with the string taut, $P$ lying on the plane and $Q$ hanging over the pulley. The particles are then released from rest.

(Take $g$ as $10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.)
incertitudes: Question 3 : le sujet imprime « Take g as 10 m s^-2 » ; valeur retenue g = 10. La longueur de la ficelle (2 m) n'intervient pas.

Question 3 (c) : on suppose que Q reste au repos au sol après le choc (pas de rebond), ce que le sujet ne précise pas ; la ficelle redevient tendue quand P repasse par la position qu'il occupait à l'instant où Q touchait le sol.

questions.enonce_markdown: Find the magnitude of the acceleration of the particles and the tension in the string.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Model.** $P$ is on the smooth plane (inclined at $\alpha$, $\sin\alpha = \tfrac35$), joined by the string over the pulley to $Q$, which hangs vertically. The forces on $P$ along the slope: the tension $T$ up the slope and the component of the weight $6g\sin\alpha$ down the slope (the normal reaction is perpendicular to the slope, no friction). The forces on $Q$: weight $4g$ down and tension $T$ up. The string is light and inextensible and the pulley is smooth, so $T$ is the same throughout and both particles have acceleration of the same magnitude $a$.

Component of $P$'s weight down the slope: $6g\sin\alpha = 6\times 10\times\tfrac35 = 36\ \mathrm{N}$. Weight of $Q$: $4g = 40\ \mathrm{N}$. Since $40 > 36$, $Q$ moves down and $P$ moves up the slope. Take the direction of motion as positive for each particle.

$$Q\ (\text{down}):\quad 40 - T = 4a$$

$$P\ (\text{up the slope}):\quad T - 36 = 6a$$

Adding the two equations eliminates $T$: $4 = 10a$, so $a = 0.4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Then $T = 36 + 6(0.4) = 38.4\ \mathrm{N}$.

(Check with $Q$: $40 - 38.4 = 1.6 = 4\times 0.4$.)

**Acceleration $= 0.4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$; tension $T = 38.4\ \mathrm{N}$.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that particle $Q$ is initially $1.5\ \mathrm{m}$ above the ground, and particle $P$ does not reach the top of the plane, calculate the speed which particle $Q$ hits the ground.
questions.corrige_markdown:
$Q$ starts from rest and descends $1.5\ \mathrm{m}$ with the constant acceleration $a = 0.4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ found in (a):

$$v^2 = u^2 + 2as = 0 + 2(0.4)(1.5) = 1.2 \;\Rightarrow\; v = \sqrt{1.2} \approx 1.10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$$

**$Q$ hits the ground with speed $\sqrt{1.2} \approx 1.10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.** At that instant $P$ is moving up the slope with the same speed.

questions.enonce_markdown: Under the conditions of part (b), calculate the time that elapses between when $Q$ reaches the ground and when the string becomes taut again.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Model.** When $Q$ reaches the ground it stops (assume no rebound), the string goes slack and the tension becomes zero. $P$ is now moving up the smooth slope at $v = \sqrt{1.2}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and the only force along the slope is the component of its weight, so (taking up the slope as positive)

$$6a' = -6g\sin\alpha \;\Rightarrow\; a' = -g\sin\alpha = -10\times\tfrac35 = -6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$$

$P$ rises, stops, and slides back down. The string becomes taut again when $P$ returns to the point it occupied when $Q$ touched the ground (the string has its full length there and $Q$ is still on the ground), i.e. when the displacement of $P$ from that point is zero:

$$0 = vt - \tfrac12(6)t^2 = t\,(v - 3t) \;\Rightarrow\; t = \frac{v}{3} = \frac{\sqrt{1.2}}{3} = \frac{\sqrt{30}}{15} \approx 0.365\ \mathrm{s}$$

(Equivalently the time up is $v/6$ and the time down is the same, total $2v/6 = v/3$.)

**The string becomes taut again after $\approx 0.365\ \mathrm{s}$.**
